claim: Sound intensity is encoded by auditory neuron subgroups that differ in thresholds and spontaneous rates.
source: Sound intensity is encoded by auditory neuron subgroups that differ in thresholds and spontaneous rates.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in auditory neuroscience presented as background information in the abstract.

claim: Intensity thresholds correlate with synaptic position on sensory hair cells.
source: Because intensity thresholds correlate with synaptic position on sensory hair cells, we combined patch clamping with fiber labeling in semi-intact cochlear preparations in neonatal rats from both sexes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge that motivated the experimental approach.

claim: The biophysical properties of auditory neurons vary in a striking spatial gradient with synaptic position.
source: The biophysical properties of auditory neurons vary in a striking spatial gradient with synaptic position.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neurons with high thresholds to injected currents contact hair cells at synaptic positions where neurons with high thresholds to sound-intensity are found in vivo.
source: Neurons with high thresholds to injected currents contact hair cells at synaptic positions where neurons with high thresholds to sound-intensity are found in vivo.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study that aligns in vitro measurements with in vivo functional properties.

claim: Alignment between in vitro and in vivo thresholds suggests that biophysical variability contributes to intensity coding.
source: Alignment between in vitro and in vivo thresholds suggests that biophysical variability contributes to intensity coding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the alignment between in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Biophysical gradients were evident at all ages examined.
source: Biophysical gradients were evident at all ages examined, indicating that cell diversity emerges in early post-natal development and persists even after continued maturation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing gradients across different postnatal ages (P1-P16).

claim: Cell diversity emerges in early post-natal development and persists even after continued maturation.
source: Biophysical gradients were evident at all ages examined, indicating that cell diversity emerges in early post-natal development and persists even after continued maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that biophysical gradients are present at all ages examined.

claim: A model for predicting synaptic position based solely on biophysical properties was remarkably successful.
source: This stability enabled a remarkably successful model for predicting synaptic position based solely on biophysical properties.
evidence: This is supported by the prediction models presented in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: In mature mammals, one inner hair cell provides input to type I spiral ganglion neurons (SGN) with different response properties (Liberman, 1982).
source: In mature mammals, one inner hair cell provides input to type I spiral ganglion neurons (SGN) with different response properties (Liberman, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liberman, 1982.

claim: Some SGN have high rates of spontaneous discharge, low-intensity thresholds and encode sound over a limited range of intensities (high-SR group).
source: Some SGN have high rates of spontaneous discharge, low-intensity thresholds and encode sound over a limited range of intensities (high-SR group).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SGN classification.

claim: Other SGN have low spontaneous rates and higher intensity thresholds (low-SR group).
source: Other SGN have low spontaneous rates and higher intensity thresholds (low-SR group).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SGN classification.

claim: High-threshold, low-SR SGN preferentially synapse on the modiolar face of an inner hair cell.
source: Specifically, these studies report an association between synaptic position on inner hair cells and intensity thresholds; wherein high-threshold, low-SR SGN preferentially synapse on the modiolar face of an inner hair cell, and low-threshold high-SR SGN synapse on the pillar face.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Kawase and Liberman, 1992; Liberman and Dodds, 1984; Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996).

claim: Low-threshold high-SR SGN synapse on the pillar face of inner hair cells.
source: Specifically, these studies report an association between synaptic position on inner hair cells and intensity thresholds; wherein high-threshold, low-SR SGN preferentially synapse on the modiolar face of an inner hair cell, and low-threshold high-SR SGN synapse on the pillar face.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pre-synaptic active zones opposing high-SR SGN have smaller ribbons than those opposing low-SR SGN (Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996).
source: For example, the pre-synaptic active zones opposing high-SR SGN have smaller ribbons (Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996) and calcium currents (Ohn et al., 2016) than those opposing low-SR SGN.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996.

claim: Pre-synaptic active zones opposing high-SR SGN have smaller calcium currents than those opposing low-SR SGN (Ohn et al., 2016).
source: For example, the pre-synaptic active zones opposing high-SR SGN have smaller ribbons (Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996) and calcium currents (Ohn et al., 2016) than those opposing low-SR SGN.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ohn et al., 2016.

claim: Large ribbons generate faster excitatory post-synaptic current (EPSC) rates in retinal ganglion cells (Mehta et al., 2013).
source: This stands in contrast to large ribbons generating faster excitatory post-synaptic current (EPSC) rates in retinal ganglion cells (Mehta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mehta et al., 2013.

claim: SGN are rich in their complements of ion channels and respond to injected currents with diverse firing patterns.
source: Previous studies in cultured spiral ganglion explants established that SGN are rich in their complements of ion channels and respond to injected currents with diverse firing patterns (Mo and Davis, 1997; Davis, 2003; Liu et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mo and Davis, 1997; Davis, 2003; Liu et al., 2014a.

claim: Type I SGN, which contact inner hair cells and are the primary conduits for sensory information, can be biophysically distinguished from type II SGNs by the kinetics of their potassium channels (Jagger and Housley, 2003).
source: For example, a previous study using semi-intact cochlear preparations reported that type I SGN, which contact inner hair cells and are the primary conduits for sensory information, can be biophysically distinguished from type II SGNs, which contact the electromotile outer hair cells, by the kinetics of their potassium channels (Jagger and Housley, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jagger and Housley, 2003.

claim: Type I SGN can be divided into genotypic subgroups based on RNA expression levels for a variety of proteins including ion channels, calcium-binding proteins and proteins affecting Ca2+ influx sensitivity (Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018; Petitpré et al., 2018; Sherrill et al., 2019).
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing studies report that type I SGN can be further divided into genotypic subgroups based on RNA expression levels for a variety of proteins including ion channels, calcium-binding proteins and proteins affecting Ca2+ influx sensitivity (Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018; Petitpré et al., 2018; Sherrill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple single-cell RNA-sequencing studies.

claim: Data were collected from spiral ganglion somata in semi-intact cochlear preparations from Long-Evans rats on post-natal day (P) one through P16.
source: Data were collected from spiral ganglion somata in semi-intact cochlear preparations from Long-Evans rats on post-natal day (P)one through P16.
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation and age range used in the study.

claim: Type I SGNs contacted inner hair cells (n = 50).
source: Type I SGNs contacted inner hair cells (Figure 1D–F; n = 50), while type II SGNs (Figure 1G; n = 9) projected underneath the inner hair cells, turned toward the cochlear base and made multiple contacts under the outer hair cells (ranging from 6 to 15 contacts).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Type II SGNs projected underneath the inner hair cells, turned toward the cochlear base and made multiple contacts under the outer hair cells (ranging from 6 to 15 contacts).
source: Type I SGNs contacted inner hair cells (Figure 1D–F; n = 50), while type II SGNs (Figure 1G; n = 9) projected underneath the inner hair cells, turned toward the cochlear base and made multiple contacts under the outer hair cells (ranging from 6 to 15 contacts).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: NBP values ranged from −0.32 to +0.52 (n = 38).
source: NBP values ranged from −0.32 to +0.52 (n = 38) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: 34 fibers were classified as modiolar-contacting, 16 fibers as pillar-contacting, and nine as type II SGN.
source: In total, we classified 34 fibers as modiolar-contacting, 16 fibers as pillar-contacting, and nine as type II SGN.
evidence: This is a summary of the classification of labeled fibers.

claim: The non-uniform distribution between Type I, Type II and subtypes of Type I fibers is in line with the pattern of innervation previously reported in rat and cat animal models (Liberman and Oliver, 1984; Kalluri and Monges-Hernandez, 2017).
source: The non-uniform distribution between Type I, Type II and subtypes of Type I fibers is in line with the pattern of innervation previously reported in rat and cat animal models, where the vast majority of SGN fibers appear to land on the modiolar-face of the inner hair cell (Liberman and Oliver, 1984; Kalluri and Monges-Hernandez, 2017).
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous studies cited.

claim: Rapidly-accommodating firing patterns were the most prevalent (n = 49).
source: Rapidly accommodating firing patterns were the most prevalent (n = 49), followed by intermediate-accommodating firing patterns (n = 19).
evidence: This is a summary of the distribution of firing patterns observed.

claim: Intermediate-accommodating firing patterns were observed in 19 neurons.
source: Rapidly accommodating firing patterns were the most prevalent (n = 49), followed by intermediate-accommodating firing patterns (n = 19).
evidence: This is a summary of the distribution of firing patterns observed.

claim: Slow-accommodating patterns were the least prevalent (n = 5), with all observations occurring between P1 and P3.
source: Slow-accommodating patterns were the least prevalent (n = 5), with all observations occurring between P1 and P3, suggesting that they might be an immature phenotype in acute preparations.
evidence: This is a summary of observations with an interpretation about developmental stage.

claim: Graded-responses were observed at all ages (n = 55).
source: Graded-responses were observed at all ages (n = 55).
evidence: This is a summary of observations across the age range studied.

claim: Current thresholds varied by spike-pattern (F(2,22.8) = 29.3, p<0.001, Welch's ANOVA).
source: Current thresholds, voltage thresholds and after hyperpolarization time-constants varied by spike-pattern (F(2,22.8) = 29.3, p<0.001; F(2,13.0) = 5.06, p=0.024; F(2,10.3) = 8.14, p=0.008, respectively by Welch's ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Voltage thresholds varied by spike-pattern (F(2,13.0) = 5.06, p=0.024, Welch's ANOVA).
source: Current thresholds, voltage thresholds and after hyperpolarization time-constants varied by spike-pattern (F(2,22.8) = 29.3, p<0.001; F(2,13.0) = 5.06, p=0.024; F(2,10.3) = 8.14, p=0.008, respectively by Welch's ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: After hyperpolarization time-constants varied by spike-pattern (F(2,10.3) = 8.14, p=0.008, Welch's ANOVA).
source: Current thresholds, voltage thresholds and after hyperpolarization time-constants varied by spike-pattern (F(2,22.8) = 29.3, p<0.001; F(2,13.0) = 5.06, p=0.024; F(2,10.3) = 8.14, p=0.008, respectively by Welch's ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Spiking-neurons as a group had more hyperpolarized resting potential than the non-spiking graded-responding neurons (−56.86 +/- 0.98 mV vs. −51.77 +/- 1.14 mV, respectively; p=0.0010, t-test).
source: Although there were no significant differences in resting potential among the three spiking neurons (potential measured in the absence of current injection; F(2,10.43) = 2.24, p=0.15, Welch's ANOVA), spiking-neurons as a group had more hyperpolarized resting potential than the non-spiking graded-responding neurons (−56.86 +/- 0.98 mV vs. −51.77 +/- 1.14 mV, respectively; p=0.0010, t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental measurements.

claim: Larger currents were needed to initiate spiking as contact positions moved from the pillar face to the modiolar face (r(20) = 0.68, p=0.0007).
source: Larger currents were needed to initiate spiking as contact positions moved from the pillar face (NBP <= 0) to the modiolar face (NBP >0) (r(20) = 0.68, p=0.0007).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Voltage thresholds hyperpolarized with increasing values of NBP (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.045).
source: Voltage thresholds hyperpolarized (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.045), resting potentials hyperpolarized (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.01) and after-hyperpolarization times became shorter with increasing values of NBP (r(20) = -0.62, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Resting potentials hyperpolarized with increasing values of NBP (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.01).
source: Voltage thresholds hyperpolarized (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.045), resting potentials hyperpolarized (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.01) and after-hyperpolarization times became shorter with increasing values of NBP (r(20) = -0.62, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: After-hyperpolarization times became shorter with increasing values of NBP (r(20) = -0.62, p<0.0001).
source: Voltage thresholds hyperpolarized (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.045), resting potentials hyperpolarized (r(20) = −0.45, p=0.01) and after-hyperpolarization times became shorter with increasing values of NBP (r(20) = -0.62, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The average NBP for intermediately-accommodating neurons is more negative than that for rapidly-accommodating neurons (−0.08 +/- 0.7 vs. 0.18 +/- 0.5, p=0.0097, test-t).
source: The average NBP for intermediately-accommodating neurons is more negative than that for rapidly-accommodating neurons (−0.08 +/- 0.7 vs. 0.18 +/- 0.5, p=0.0097, test-t).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental measurements.

claim: Response latencies of graded/non-spiking and spiking-neurons are faster for fiber-contact positions closer to the modiolar face of the inner hair cell (r(34) = −0.74, p<0.0001, pooled).
source: The response latencies of graded/non-spiking and spiking-neurons are faster for fiber-contact positions closer to themodiolar face of the inner hair cell (r(34) = −0.74, p<0.0001, pooled; r(20)=-0.65, p=0.0013, spiking; r(14)=-0.89, p<0.0001, non-spiking).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mean latency was not significantly different between spiking and non-spiking groups (p=0.94, ANCOVA).
source: Analysis of co-variance confirmed that the mean latency was not significantly different between spiking and non-spiking groups (p=0.94, ANCOVA,Table 1 ).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: The slope of the regression was not significantly different between spiking and non-spiking neurons (p=0.71, ANCOVA).
source: Nor was the slope of the regression significantly different between spiking and non-spiking neurons (p=0.71, ANCOVA, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: The number of terminal branches decreases as a function of maturation (r(53) = −0.79, p<0.0001).
source: Consistent with previous reports, we also found that the number of terminal branches decreases as a function of maturation (r(53) = −0.79, p<0.0001) (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of morphological data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mature one-to-one connections were observed as early as P5 on the modiolar face.
source: We observed mature one-to-one connections as early as P5 on the modiolar face.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the morphological data.

claim: None of the pillar-contacting fibers had mature terminal morphology, even by P10.
source: In contrast, none of the pillar-contacting fibers had mature terminal morphology, even by P10 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the morphological data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Modiolar-contacting fibers have fewer branches than pillar-contacting fibers from P5-P10 (1.9 +/- 0.24, n = 12 vs. 3.2 +/- 0.32, n = 7, respectively; p=0.030, t-test).
source: We quantified differences in the pruning rate of modiolar- and pillar-contacting fibers from P5-P10 and found that modiolar-contacting fibers' have fewer branches than do pillar-contacting fibers (1.9 +/- 0.24, n = 12 vs. 3.2 +/- 0.32, n = 7, respectively) (p=0.030, t-test) (Figure 7C, inset).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of morphological measurements.

claim: Type I SGN have significantly larger fiber diameters than type II SGN (1.28 +/- 0.05 µm, n = 37 vs. 0.59 +/- 0.12 µm, n = 6; p<0.0001, t-test).
source: Consistent with previous in vivo labeling studies, we found that type I SGN have significantly larger fiber diameters than do type II SGN (1.28 +/- 0.05 µm, n = 37 vs. 0.59 +/- 0.12 µm, n = 6; p<0.0001, t-test) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of morphological measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Fiber diameters are not significantly different between modiolar-contacting SGN and pillar-contacting SGN (1.25 +/- 0.29 µm vs. 1.11 +/- 0.22 µm; p=0.25, t-test).
source: Fiber diameters are not significantly different between modiolar-contacting SGN and pillar-contacting SGN (1.25 +/- 0.29 µm vs. 1.11 +/- 0.22 µm; p=0.25, t-test) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of morphological measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Maximum whole-cell conductance (gmax) increased as a function of NBP (r(34) = 0.57, p=0.0003).
source: Maximum whole-cell conductance (gmax) increased as a function of NBP (r(34) = 0.57, p=0.0003) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Neurons terminating on the modiolar-face had large g-30, suggesting that they may have had larger low-voltage gated components (r(34) = 0.64, p<0.0001).
source: Neurons terminating on the modiolar-face also had large g-30, suggesting that they may have had larger low-voltage gated components (r(34) = 0.64, p<0.0001) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis with an interpretation about ion channel properties.

claim: V1/2 was not significantly correlated to basal position (r(34) = −0.23, p=0.17).
source: However, V1/2 was not significantly correlated to basal position (r(34) = −0.23, p=0.17) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Inactivation time constant was correlated with normalized basal position, with the largest time constants found for neurons on the modiolar face of the inner hair cell (r(25) = 0.50, p=0.0087).
source: Inactivation time constant was correlated with normalized basal position; with the largest time constants found for neurons on the modiolar face of the inner hair cell (r(25) = 0.50, p=0.0087).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of voltage-clamp data.

claim: The best prediction model for spiking-neurons included three variables: current threshold, gmax, and τinact, and accounted for 75% of the variance in the data (adjusted-R2 = 0.75, p=0.0004).
source: The model (Table 3) accounted for 75% of the variance in the data (adjusted- R2 = 0.75, p=0.0004) and accurately predicted the basal position within approximately +/- 9% margin of error (RMSE = 0.092).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the multiple regression model shown in Figure 5A and Table 3.

claim: The model for spiking-neurons accurately predicted the basal position within approximately +/- 9% margin of error (RMSE = 0.092).
source: The model (Table 3) accounted for 75% of the variance in the data (adjusted- R2 = 0.75, p=0.0004) and accurately predicted the basal position within approximately +/- 9% margin of error (RMSE = 0.092).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the multiple regression model.

claim: Using response latency as the sole input variable for the model at P3-P5 accounts for 55% of the variance in the data (R2 = 0.55, p=0.0010) and predicts the basal position within a 12.3% margin of error (RMSE = 0.123).
source: Using response latency as the sole input variable for the model at P3-P5 accounts for 55% of the variance in the data (R2 = 0.55, p=0.0010) and predicts the basal position within a 12.3% margin of error (RMSE = 0.123) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the regression model for a specific age range shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At P6-P8, response latency accounted for 55% of the variance (R2 = 0.55, p=0.0003) and predicted the basal position within a 14% margin of error (RMSE = 0.140).
source: At P6-P8, response latency, resting potentials, g-30, and gmax were all significantly correlated with the basal position (Table 2). Response latency still accounted for 55% of the variance (R2 = 0.55, p=0.0003) and predicted the basal position within a 14% margin of error (RMSE = 0.140) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the regression model for a specific age range shown in Figure 5D.

claim: gmax becomes larger with age (r(136) = 0.50, p<0.0001).
source: The three key predictors for NBP change significantly with age; gmax becomes larger (r(136) = 0.50, p<0.0001), current thresholds increase (r(79)=0.42, p<0.0001), and average latencies become shorter (r(133)=-0.40, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis showing age-dependent changes.

claim: Current thresholds increase with age (r(79)=0.42, p<0.0001).
source: The three key predictors for NBP change significantly with age; gmax becomes larger (r(136) = 0.50, p<0.0001), current thresholds increase (r(79)=0.42, p<0.0001), and average latencies become shorter (r(133)=-0.40, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis showing age-dependent changes.

claim: Average latencies become shorter with age (r(133)=-0.40, p<0.0001).
source: The three key predictors for NBP change significantly with age; gmax becomes larger (r(136) = 0.50, p<0.0001), current thresholds increase (r(79)=0.42, p<0.0001), and average latencies become shorter (r(133)=-0.40, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis showing age-dependent changes.

claim: There was a significant interaction between the effects of age and synaptic position (modiolar/pillar) on gmax (Class*Age: F(1,33)=5.98, p=0.0199, ANCOVA).
source: There was also a significant interaction between the effects of age and synaptic position (modiolar/pillar) on gmax (Class*Age: F(1,33)=5.98, p=0.0199, ANCOVA; Table 1, Table 4).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis showing differential developmental trajectories.

claim: gmax is on average larger and grows nearly twice as fast with age for modiolar-contacting SGN than for pillar-contacting SGN.
source: As evident in Figure 6C, gmax is on average larger and grows nearly twice as fast with age for modiolar-contacting SGN than for pillar-contacting SGN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is a significant interaction between the effects of age and synaptic position on latency (F(1,33)=8.4, p=0.0066, ANCOVA).
source: As with gmax, there is also a significant interaction between the effects of age and synaptic position on latency (F(1,33)=8.4, p=0.0066, ANCOVA, Table 1, Table 4).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis showing differential developmental trajectories.

claim: This is the first study to demonstrate an alignment between the intrinsic properties of spiral ganglion neurons and their function.
source: This is the first study to demonstrate such an alignment between the intrinsic properties of spiral ganglion neurons and their function.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: Biophysical diversity is not a transient feature of immaturity and likely persists to influence mature function.
source: Biophysical diversity is not a transient feature of immaturity and likely persists to influence mature function.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the persistence of biophysical gradients across ages.

claim: The coefficient of variation for the distributions of biophysical features does not change with maturation.
source: The coefficient of variation (a measure of relative dispersion) for the distributions of biophysical features does not change with maturation.
evidence: This is a statistical observation about the relative dispersion of biophysical properties across ages.

claim: The molecular and transcriptomic profile of SGN changes during development to eventually stabilize into distinct subtypes (Petitpré et al., 2018; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
source: Consistent with this result, single-cell RNA sequencing recently demonstrated that the molecular and transcriptomic profile of SGN changes during development to eventually stabilize into distinct subtypes (Petitpré et al., 2018; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to single-cell RNA sequencing studies.

claim: Firing patterns become more rapidly accommodating and first-spike latencies are on average faster by the end of the second post-natal week, more so in fibers contacting the high-frequency-encoding basal turn of the cochlea than in the low-frequency-encoding apical turn (Crozier and Davis, 2014; Adamson et al., 2002).
source: By the end of the second post-natal week, firing patterns are more rapidly accommodating and first-spike latencies are on average faster than in the first week; more so in fibers contacting the high-frequency-encoding basal turn of the cochlea than in the low-frequency-encoding apical turn (Crozier and Davis, 2014; Adamson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The pruning of dendritic branches to form a one-terminal-contact is a well-described morphological hallmark of maturing auditory neurons (Echteler, 1992; Barclay et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2007).
source: The pruning of dendritic branches to form a one-terminal-contact is a well-described morphological hallmark of maturing auditory neurons (Echteler, 1992; Barclay et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Modiolar-contacting fibers appear to be less enriched for the calcium-binding protein, calretinin, than pillar-contacting fibers in mature rats (Kalluri and Monges-Hernandez, 2017) and mice (e.g. Shrestha et al., 2018).
source: Evidence from the literature further supports this suggestion; for example, modiolar-contacting fibers appear to be less enriched for the calcium-binding protein, calretinin, than pillar-contacting fibers in mature rats (Kalluri and Monges-Hernandez, 2017) and mice (e.g. Shrestha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High-spontaneous-rate/low-threshold responses (prevalent for fibers on the pillar face) emerge later in development than do low-spontaneous-rate/high-threshold responses (Wu et al., 2016).
source: That pillar-contacting fibers may be developing at a slower rate is consistent with the observation that high-spontaneous-rate/low-threshold responses (prevalent for fibers on the pillar face) emerge later in development than do low-spontaneous-rate/high-threshold responses (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: The presence of growth factors such as BDNF and NT-3 (typically released by hair cells and supporting cells in situ) has a profound influence on firing patterns and expression of proteins for ion channels and receptors (e.g. Flores-Otero et al., 2007; Sun and Salvi, 2009).
source: In cultured SGN, the presence of growth factors such as BDNF and NT-3 (typically released by hair cells and supporting cells in situ) has a profound influence on firing patterns and expression of proteins for ion channels and receptors (e.g. Flores-Otero et al., 2007; Sun and Salvi, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Post-natal diversification fails in the absence of synaptic input (Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
source: That extrinsic signals may influence SGN diversity is further strengthened by recent findings that post-natal diversification fails in the absence of synaptic input (Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: In zebrafish, the presence of afferent fibers is crucial for the formation and stabilization of synaptic ribbons in the hair cell (Suli et al., 2016).
source: In zebrafish, the presence of afferent fibers is crucial for the formation and stabilization of synaptic ribbons in the hair cell (Suli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suli et al., 2016.

claim: Spatial gradients in the voltage dependence of pre-synaptic calcium channels is controlled by the enhanced expression of the Pou4f1 transcription factor in modiolar-contacting SGN (Sherrill et al., 2019).
source: In mice, Sherrill et al., 2019 recently reported that spatial gradients in the voltage dependence of pre-synaptic calcium channels is controlled by the enhanced expression of the Pou4f1 transcription factor in modiolar-contacting SGN.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sherrill et al., 2019.

claim: Rapidly accommodating neurons have faster latencies, higher current thresholds and larger low-voltage gated potassium currents in cultured neurons (Mo and Davis, 1997; Chen and Davis, 2006; Liu and Davis, 2014b; Lv et al., 2010).
source: These findings are consistent with SGN biophysics in cultured neurons, where rapidly accommodating neurons have faster latencies, higher current thresholds and larger low-voltage gated potassium currents (Mo and Davis, 1997; Chen and Davis, 2006; Liu and Davis, 2014b; Lv et al., 2010).
